Came here to say this. The songs are all amazing, the tracks roll together perfectly, it is as much of an experience as it is an album.

If you want to fully experience the glory that is DSOTM, I would suggest taking a lazy afternoon and listening to the entire Pink Floyd discography. Its quite a trip (sometimes literally).

That journey begins with the irreplaceable Syd Barrett, and in those early songs (e.g. "Set the controls for the heart of the sun") you can get a glimpse of the epic prog jams that will define the late 70s. But the lyrics and tone of Syd Barrett are unmistakable, and although he can certainly be "hit or miss" depending on the track (I think "The Gnome" is genius, some hate it) his influence on all music that would follow cannot be overstated.

Of course, with "Ummagumma" the story changes- Syd gets very sick, and fully loses his mind. This theme of insanity will be a core concept on DSOTM, and obviously influence the follow-up "Wish You Were Here". Waters will ultimately come face-to-face with his own fear of going insane, just as his dear friend Syd (real name Roger) did, in "The Trial" which is of course the finale of the Wall. But that all comes later...

The second half of Ummagumma shows a band in crisis. Much like the Beatles "White Album", each piece was composed more or less independently of the other band members. Most famous from this set is "Several Species of Small Furry Animals Gathered Together in a Cave and Grooving with a Pict" or as I prefer to call it "Roger Waters does a lousy Syd Barrett impression while having fun with his schoolteacher voice character". I think the best work of the second half of Ummagumma clearly belongs to David Gilmour.

The next few albums "More" and "Atom Heart Mother" show a band eager to experiment, dripping with ambition, but still painfully shy and unsure of themselves. By the time "Meddle" comes around, we can hear via "Echoes" (the longest single track in the entire PF discography) that this is a band that has become something even more following the passing of the Barrett-era. This period of work remains sluggish, and at times, blatantly self-indulgent (or if you prefer, "experimental"). But the most telling feature of this era is that the band is still comprised of EQUALS who still genuinely admire and respect each other. The coming rise of Roger's ego, and the inevitable Gilmour-Waters battle (and subsequent death of the band) are still more than a decade away.

This takes us to "Obscured By Clouds", recorded in tandem with DSOTM and perhaps the "catchier" of the two. Here we see Roger's lyrics have blossomed into true poetry, matched by a band that remains passionate and eager to take risks, willing to share the spotlight with one another for the greater good of a song.

And then, as the soft, slow drum beat (heartbeat) fades in, and the first glorious notes of DSOTM begin, it is as if all the pieces of the entire universe finally fall together in perfect harmony, if only for 45 minutes. The once sloppy, self-indulgent band has become an efficient, dangerously calibrated machine. Every song is a masterpiece, none outstay their welcome, and they all belong together, and in doing so, form a crystal clear narrative on life, the universe, and everything.

Yes, friends, DSOTM is clearly the best album ever made. 1973 was a very special time for music. The "Baby Boomers" who would go on to destroy the economy and environment were still wide-eyed kids. And Pink Floyd, the band that would go on to spend the majority of the 80's in vicious litigation thanks to Roger Waters crippling insecurity was still a group of equals, making something greater than the sum of its parts.

Plus, if you don't get chills during "Great Gig In The Sky" then I'm pretty sure you're either a sociopath or a robot.
